talks.title: Adversaries abuse OAuth applications with diverse TTPs to automate attacks
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Adversaries abuse OAuth applications with diverse TTPs to automate attacks.
talks.summary: Adversaries abuse OAuth applications with diverse TTPs to automate attacks.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Venkat and Charlene Dave, cloud application threat researchers at Microsoft, present an analysis of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) targeting OAuth applications across cloud enterprise environments. Highlighting an industry shift where threat actors transition from compromising users and devices to exploiting application identities, the speakers explain how cloud app permissions are weaponized for persistent access and automated exploitation. Through detailed case studies of real-world campaigns from 2019 to 2023, the researchers dissect consent phishing, automated email laundry, business email compromise (BEC), and unauthorized cryptocurrency mining orchestrated via compromised OAuth applications.

Key Topics:
- The threat model shift from user/device identity to cloud application context
- Illicit OAuth consent phishing campaigns leveraging brand impersonation and multi-tenant applications
- Automated email laundering using Exchange transport rules, inbound connectors, and Graph API
- High-volume business email compromise (BEC) and cloud resource hijacking for cryptocurrency mining

Technical Details:
OAuth 2.0 relies on token-based authorization between client applications, resource owners, authorization servers, and resource servers. Because enterprise SaaS environments often lack visibility into third-party cloud apps, adversaries exploit the transition from user context to application context. In consent phishing campaigns (such as the 2020 SANS breach), attackers send emails directing victims to an OAuth consent screen. Once approved, the stolen access token grants high-privilege scopes like MailboxSettings.ReadWrite and Files.ReadWrite. Attackers evade detection by impersonating legitimate brand names and corporate logos. They execute keyword searches across emails, configure inbox forwarding rules to exfiltrate sensitive messages, and delete trace logs. Advanced variants use HTML redirector attachments, host malicious multi-tenant apps in attacker tenants, and enumerate directories via Microsoft Graph.

The speakers also detail 'automated email laundry' campaigns designed for high-volume spam delivery. Attackers compromise administrative accounts via password spraying against tenants lacking MFA. In one variant, the attacker leverages Exchange Administrator privileges to run PowerShell commands establishing inbound connectors and transport rules. These transport rules strip or alter email headers, routing outbound spam through legitimate corporate infrastructure to evade external filters. In a second variant, attackers generate OAuth application certificates or assign compromised accounts as service principal owners, weaponizing the Mail.Send Graph API permission to blast high-volume spam externally and internally.

In Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks, adversaries harvest credentials using adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing pages replicating corporate branding, followed by session token replay. The actor registers a multi-tenant OAuth application in Azure with broad Graph API scopes (Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send, User.Read). To evade detection, the actor creates a hidden inbox rule using suspicious punctuation (such as '....') to route incoming security alerts to Junk and mark them as read. The OAuth app is then used to blast over 3,500 phishing emails, query /me/people to map contacts, and exfiltrate sensitive emails. Finally, attackers deploy OAuth apps for cryptocurrency mining: gaining access via leaked VPN credentials, the attacker elevates an application to Contributor under a compromised Azure subscription, adds client secrets, and deploys large VM clusters named with a <domain>-<region> pattern to blend in with enterprise workloads.

Key Takeaways:
Securing cloud environments requires extending identity perimeters beyond users and devices to encompass cloud applications and service principals. Organizations must enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) across all administrative accounts to block password spraying, and deploy Conditional Access policies based on device health and IP reputation. Security teams must enforce strict app hygiene by identifying and disabling dormant applications, revoking unused or expiring credentials, and restricting administrative consent workflows. Furthermore, organizations should audit high-privilege Microsoft Graph permissions, monitor suspicious inbox rules featuring abnormal naming patterns, and scrutinize Exchange Online ApplicationImpersonation assignments.
